_README: Visa, customs, health, safety, police, legal and photography rules as DK 2015 states them (Survival Guide pp270–275, hotel check-in p233). Paraphrase only. facts.json and corrections.json are the published truth; every disagreement is marked conflict and logged in ../disputes.md.

visa.claim: In 2015 visas came from embassies (best via an agency) or by 'visa on arrival': an online approval letter plus a US$45 stamping fee paid at the airport. Tourist visas were one month, three months cost little more; business visas needed a sponsor letter.
visa.conflict_with: facts.json visa.type / visa.fee / visa.max_stay_days: Americans use the e-visa (US$25 single, US$50 multiple, up to 90 days) at evisa.gov.vn; the VOA approval-letter trade is the intermediary market corrections #4 and disputes.md warn about

visa.claim: Citizens of some neighbouring countries got waivers on arrival of varying length.
visa.note: Consistent with corrections #5: the US has never been on the unilateral exemption list.

visa.claim: Hotels take the passport at check-in to register the guest with police; big-city hotels may copy and return it; a photocopy is 'usually acceptable' if the passport is at an embassy.
visa.verify_against: facts.json documents.police_registration (verified duty); current hotel practice is photograph-and-return
visa.note: corrections #7: never state a consequence for non-registration.

visa.claim: Renting a private room or apartment long-term also requires police registration.

LP 2016 visa picture: 'very complicated… fluid — always check'. Fifteen-day exemptions for a list of European and Asian nationalities, 30 days for ASEAN, none for the USA, Australia or New Zealand; exemption users cannot extend and cannot re-enter on exemption within 30 days; tourist visas of 30 or 90 days; online agents sold a visa-on-arrival approval letter (airports only) as 'the preferred method for most travellers arriving by air'; embassies slower and dearer.
visa.conflict_with: facts.json visa.* — the e-visa (2017 pilot, 90-day multi-entry from Aug 2023) replaced the letter; the agents named are now the intermediary market our visa articles warn about

visa.claim: LP 2016 on extensions: 'if you've got the dollars, they've got the rubber stamp' — officially cheap, arranged only via agents, about seven days, 30 or 90 days depending on the visa, dearer if done in a different city from arrival, smoothest in HCMC, Hanoi, Danang and Hue.
visa.conflict_with: corrections.json #4 and facts.json visa.no_extension_in_country: an e-visa cannot be extended in-country; intermediaries selling e-visa extensions sell something the government says does not exist. The 2016 picture applied to embassy/VOA visas.

visa.claim: To pop into Cambodia or Laos and return you must already hold a multiple-entry visa before leaving Vietnam; LP 2016 said agents in Hanoi/HCMC could convert a single to multiple for a fee in up to seven days.
visa.verify_against: facts.json: choose multiple-entry at e-visa application; no in-country conversion

visa.claim: Passports are almost always requested at check-in; LP says handing it over is not absolutely essential but at minimum a photocopy of the passport details and visa is needed, because the government strictly regulates registering foreigners overnight — which is also why every homestay must be officially licensed.

customs.claim: 2015 allowance: 1.5 litres of alcohol and 400 cigarettes; declare gold over 300 g and cash over US$5,000; a yellow customs-form copy was handed back.
customs.conflict_with: facts.json customs.tobacco = 200 cigarettes / 250 g / 20 cigars (Decree 134/2016); customs.alcohol tiers 1.5 L ≥20% ABV, 2 L <20%, 3 L beer; the US$5,000 / 15,000,000 VND cash declaration matches documents.currency_declaration; the yellow form no longer exists

customs.claim: Few foreigners are searched, but material judged politically sensitive or pornographic — including media critical of the government — can be seized.
All outbound parcels, including courier shipments and packets of CDs or photographs, are opened and inspected before leaving the country, which is why parcels take months.
customs.verify_against: Vietnam Post / DHL current export inspection practice

customs.claim: Some restaurants serve wild species such as porcupine despite an official ban.
customs.note: US readers may also face US import rules on wildlife products — out of the book's scope.

customs.claim: LP 2016 duty limits: 400 cigarettes, 1.5 litres of spirits, declare US$5,000 or more.
customs.conflict_with: facts.json customs.tobacco = 200 cigarettes (Decree 134/2016); both 2015–16 books carry the old 400 figure

customs.claim: Vietnamese black peppercorns are a fine edible souvenir 'if your country will allow it in'; US CBP admits commercially packaged dried spices — a good ingredients-to-bring-home item. Snake wine is the opposite: the snakes are often protected species and the bottle is a wildlife product.
customs.verify_against: CBP 'bringing food into the US' rules; CITES

health.claim: WHO-recommended for SE Asia: hepatitis A and B, tetanus, MMR, diphtheria, typhoid.
health.verify_against: facts.json safety_health.vaccines_recommended (CDC list, verified) — CDC is the source we publish

health.claim: Malaria 'eradicated from most of the country', slight risk on Phu Quoc and in highland areas; prophylaxis if visiting jungle areas or the Mekong, doctor's advice first.
health.conflict_with: facts.json safety_health.malaria (CDC): rural transmission only, rare in the deltas, none in the main cities; CDC does not single out Phu Quoc. CDC wins.

health.claim: Dengue is the serious mosquito risk, with no vaccine in 2015; repellent and nets; biting peaks dusk and dawn; fan/A-C rooms have fewer mosquitoes.
health.verify_against: CDC Vietnam page: dengue vaccine (Qdenga) exists but is not routinely recommended for travellers

health.claim: Hospitals may refuse treatment without proof of ability to pay; care outside HCMC/Hanoi is poor; serious cases go to Bangkok, Singapore or Hong Kong; insurance must cover medevac and theft.
City pharmacies are well stocked but check expiry dates; bring your own supply of anything specific.

Diarrhoea, dysentery and giardia are the common ailments; wash hands, eat where food is cooked in front of you, peel fruit yourself, be wary even of five-star buffets and room service; bottled or boiled water; tea is safe.
Bird flu, swine flu and hand-foot-and-mouth (children) have recurred since 2005; avoid the caged 'release' birds sold at temples.
Cuts infect quickly in the climate; carry disinfectant and dressings.
Hydrate, hat, sunglasses, loose clothes, sunscreen; the Feb–Apr hot season is the dangerous one.
LP's tap-water box: urban tap water is heavily chlorinated but still avoid it; bottled water everywhere; ice is generally safe in cities and resorts and is routinely added to drinks and coffee.
health.verify_against: CDC Vietnam page 'do not drink tap water'; ice from commercial producers
health.note: Resolves the direction of disputes.md tap_water_safe: no to tap, yes to city ice.

health.claim: LP 2016: enormous misinformation about malaria; minimal-to-no risk in cities and resorts including Danang, Hanoi, HCMC and Nha Trang; in most rural areas the risk outweighs tablet side effects; isolated high-risk areas named as Ca Mau and Bac Lieu provinces and the rural south; doxycycline, mefloquine (~90%, psychiatric side effects) and Malarone (best for divers and short trips) discussed; standby treatment is a weak option.
health.verify_against: facts.json safety_health.malaria (CDC) governs: rural only, rare in the deltas, none in the main cities

health.claim: The dengue mosquito bites by day as well as night, so repellent is an all-day measure; several hundred thousand hospitalisations a year in Vietnam, fatality under 0.3%; treat with rest and paracetamol, never aspirin.

Travellers' diarrhoea hits 30–50% of visitors within two weeks; over 80% is bacterial and responds to antibiotics; loperamide is only a 'stopper' for bus days and must not be used with fever or blood; restaurants are the biggest risk factor — fresh-cooked food, avoid shellfish and buffets, peel fruit, busy high-turnover places.

Private clinics first (Hanoi, HCMC, Danang near developed-country standard, can organise evacuation); state hospitals overcrowded and basic and need a special licence to treat foreigners, which few hold; for surgery fly to Bangkok, Singapore or Hong Kong; evacuation bills of US$100,000 are 'not unknown'; fake and expired over-the-counter drugs are common.

Rabies is uniformly fatal; dogs and monkeys are the usual source; wash the bite, apply iodine, start post-exposure treatment immediately; pre-travel vaccination greatly simplifies treatment because immunoglobulin is scarce.

Take it easy on arrival; rehydration solution and salty food; heatstroke above 41°C is an emergency; sunburn happens on cloudy days — SPF 30+, hat, avoid 10am–2pm; sunscreen is scarce and dear in Vietnam, bring it.
LP's framing: travellers worry about infections, but accidental injury — above all traffic — accounts for most life-threatening problems; serious infectious illness is rare, minor sickness common.

The only vaccination required by regulation is yellow fever, and only if you were in a yellow-fever zone within six days of arrival; WHO's recommended list (hep A and B, tetanus/diphtheria booster, MMR, typhoid, varicella; JE, rabies, meningitis and TB testing for long stays) matches the CDC list in facts.json.

Pregnant travellers: second trimester ideal; avoid remote areas; insurance must cover premature labour; no antimalarial is fully safe; azithromycin is the safe diarrhoea treatment; bring birth control as options are limited.

safety.claim: The book calls Vietnam 'one of the safest places to travel in the world': authoritarian state, law-abiding society, rising petty crime in big cities, rare violent crime.
safety.note: Matches facts.json safety_health.main_risk and the Level 1 advisory.

safety.claim: Motorbike-mounted thieves snatch bags, phones and cameras from pedestrians and pillion riders in HCMC and Nha Trang especially; money belt, hotel safe, photocopies of documents.
A specific HCMC con: friendly strangers in District 1 invite you home or for coffee, leading to a rigged card game run by a Filipino gang.
safety.verify_against: Still reported on forums; check for a current US Embassy mention

safety.claim: Tourist police at major sites are 'generally just for show'; general police may refuse to file a theft report; be polite, bring an interpreter.
safety.note: Consistent with facts.json safety_health.consular_access on slow official processes.

safety.claim: Unexploded ordnance remains a concern in the DMZ; tourist areas are cleared; never touch anything that looks like a shell.
Solo foreign women are common; rural staring is curiosity; invitations home happen; dress modestly; normal night precautions.
Attitudes liberalised over the decade before 2015; HCMC has a thriving gay scene.
The timeline records a US citizen jailed in 2012 for pro-democracy activity, journalists expelled, and blocked social media — the state tolerates religion and commerce, not political dissent.

LP: 'an extremely safe country'; police keep a tight grip on social order; muggings, robberies and sexual assaults rarely reported; scams and hassles concentrated in Hanoi, HCMC and Nha Trang, less in Hoi An; vendor hustle in Hue, Sapa and tourist beaches, none off the track; the single most important precaution is extra care on two wheels.

UXO: an estimated 150,000 tonnes left at war's end; more than 40,000 Vietnamese maimed or killed since 1975; the central provinces worst, over 8,000 incidents in Quang Tri alone; cities, farmland and travelled paths are safe, straying is not; never touch relics or climb into bomb craters; don't leave established trekking paths.
safety.note: Consistent with facts.json safety_health.uxo; figures are LP's, 2016.

safety.claim: 'Hotels from hell': a well-reviewed hotel spawns a copycat with the same name down the road, and taxi drivers deliver arrivals to the fake one — Hanoi especially; check the room before checking in; some Hanoi hotels harass guests to book tours.
Big riptides run along the main coastline; flags and lifeguards only at popular beaches; test the current at quiet beaches; Phu Quoc's seas are more sheltered.
Jellyfish (travel in groups — look before leaping; vinegar on stings), stonefish, scorpion fish and stingrays in the shallows — plastic shoes help; risk small.

Children attract overwhelming attention, especially blond or blue-eyed babies — cheek pinching and, rarely, groin-grabbing of small boys — 'keep them close'; no car seats in taxis or rental cars; cots only in mid/top hotels; the real hazard is hand-to-mouth with dysentery, typhoid and hepatitis around — bring hand gel.

Foreigners rarely get police hassle and bribe demands are very rare; after a theft the police can do little beyond an insurance report 'for a negotiable fee' — bring an English-speaking Vietnamese; many plain-clothes police; drug arrests mean a large fine, a long sentence or both.

Relatively free of serious hassles; thousands of women travel alone each year; society does not expect women to be subordinate; East-Asian-looking women with Western men may very occasionally be taken for sex workers by 'ill-educated locals'; sleeveless tops draw attention away from the beach.

No laws against same-sex relations; VietPride marches since 2012 (Hanoi late July/early August); a 2015 marriage law allows but does not recognise gay weddings; discreet scenes in both cities; same-sex hotel check-in fine; no public affection for anyone.
Many policies exclude motorbiking, diving and even trekking — check; evacuation cover is essential; driving a vehicle requires a Vietnamese insurance policy.

legal_and_practical.claim: No photography of military areas or police stations; ask before photographing people (especially ethnic minorities) and religious sites.
Helmets are mandatory; two people max per motorbike, inconsistently enforced.
legal_and_practical.note: facts.json getting_around.traffic_laws adds zero-alcohol and tightening enforcement.

legal_and_practical.claim: All media censored; some websites blocked permanently, others intermittently; the post office inspects parcels.
legal_and_practical.verify_against: Facebook/Google accessible today; some news sites still blocked; VPN use common

legal_and_practical.claim: Betting legal only on greyhounds and horses in 2015.
legal_and_practical.verify_against: Vung Tau dog track closed; casinos admit foreign passport holders

legal_and_practical.claim: 220 V; most sockets take both French round and US flat two-pin plugs; hotels lend adapters; charge daily because small-town outages happen.
UTC+7, 12 h ahead of US Eastern Standard, 15 h ahead of Pacific Standard; Gregorian calendar official, lunar for religion.
Public toilets rare; attended pay toilets in central HCMC; Hoi An has the most; squat toilets exist; carry paper and bin it rather than flush.
Addresses read number, street, district (HCMC); a slash (120/5) means alley beside no. 120, building 5; numbering restarts at district lines; the word for street precedes the name.

Wheelchair users face vendor-blocked sidewalks (the kerb ramps are for motorbikes), few lifts, almost no accessible toilets; only new luxury hotels are equipped; agencies can hire an untrained helper.
legal_and_practical.note: No accessibility article exists — see coverage-gaps.md.

legal_and_practical.claim: Vietnamese rise early and 'consider sleeping in a sure indication of illness'; lunch is sacred — virtually everything shuts noon to 1.30pm and government offices 11.30 to 2; Saturday mornings open, Sundays closed; museums often shut Mondays.

No photographs of airports, military bases or border checkpoints, and 'don't even think of' photographing Ho Chi Minh in his sarcophagus; with hill-tribe people ask first, accept no, and send the photo if you promise one.

Government 'tourist offices' (Vietnam Tourism, Saigon Tourist and provincial equivalents) are travel agencies selling tours, not information desks; agents, backpacker cafés and other travellers are better sources.
220 V 50 Hz, very rarely 110 V; sockets usually take two round pins (LP) — DK adds flat US pins also fit; bring an adapter either way.

If there is a bin beside the toilet the paper goes in the bin; no bin, flush; paper provided except at bus and train stations; squat toilets persist in public and rural places; scarcity hits women harder; a sarong makes roadside stops easier.

Not easy for wheelchair users: chaotic traffic, pavements blocked by parked bikes and stalls, bathroom doorways too narrow for chairs over 60 cm; some budget and most mid/top hotels have lifts; trains are not geared for wheelchairs but open-tour buses are doable; a private car and driver makes almost anywhere accessible; Vietnamese are always willing to help lift; blind travellers need a sighted companion for the traffic.
legal_and_practical.note: Still no accessibility article; see coverage-gaps.

legal_and_practical.claim: A smoker's paradise and a non-smoker's nightmare despite an official ban in public places; air-con transport is effectively smoke-free.
Vietnam News is 'propagandist'; Voice of Vietnam is pumped through loudspeakers in rural towns and parts of Hanoi — the dawn loudspeaker is real; listings magazines come and go.
In cities you cannot turn right on a red light — a specifically American habit to unlearn.
legal_and_practical.verify_against: Road Traffic Law; some junctions now have green right-turn arrows

legal_and_practical.claim: Cheap Lonely Planet guides sold on the street are pirated copies — 'if it's cheap, it's a copy'.

Excellent, comprehensive cellular network; three carriers — Viettel, Vinaphone, Mobifone — with offices nationwide; local SIMs 'extremely cheap'; LP 2016 said the GSM bands were incompatible with North American phones, which is no longer true of modern handsets.
Wifi in about 98% of hotels and guesthouses, free except at some five-stars; cafés and restaurants too; speeds fine for everything but streaming (2016).

LP's 2016 public-holiday list: Jan 1; Tet (three days); Feb 3; Hung Kings (10th of 3rd moon); Apr 30; May 1; May 19; Sep 2; weekend holidays observed on Monday. It wrongly adds Buddha's birthday as a holiday on the 8th of the 4th moon.
